idiom_name: framework-owned state slots plus effect registration composed in a plain function
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the host runtime provides per-call-site state storage keyed by invocation order and an effect mechanism whose callbacks run and are cancelled with the host's lifetime. The unit is a plain function that reads and writes those slots, registers effects for anything outside the runtime (subscriptions, timers, I/O), and returns state values plus stable action callbacks; units compose by calling one another. Nothing in the unit may depend on the host's markup, and no state may be shared implicitly between call sites — shared state belongs to a store or context object. Where the ecosystem has no host runtime, the closest structure is a state-holder object or closure pair plus the framework's observer/signal mechanism.
code_sketch:
function useOnlineStatus():
    state = host.stateSlot(True)          # per-call-site slot, keyed by call order
    host.effect(setup=subscribe(state), cleanup=unsubscribe)
    return state.value

component StatusBar:
    online = useOnlineStatus()            # independent instance per call site
    render(online ? 'Online' : 'Disconnected')
pitfalls: Calling the unit outside the host's render, or conditionally, breaks slot identity and cross-wires state.
Sharing one state instance between call sites turns an instance-local helper into an accidental singleton.
Returning unstable closures that capture stale state makes effects and listeners observe the past.
Omitting the SSR guard when the body reads window/document causes server-render crashes.
Silencing exhaustive-deps lint instead of fixing effect dependencies produces stale-closure bugs.

Wrong move: returning a fresh object or array literal on every render -> consumers' React.memo and useMemo collapse because shallow comparison only checks references, so dependent components re-render even when nothing changed -> instead return primitives, memoise the returned shape with useMemo/useCallback, or enable the React Compiler.

Wrong move: extracting a hook just to shorten a long component -> hidden state, invisible dependencies and cross-file jumps replace the readability problem the extraction was meant to solve -> instead restructure the component first and extract only when the same stateful logic exists in two or more real consumers.

Wrong move: creating JSX elements inside the unit's body so the hook 'owns' the UI -> the element is rebuilt every render, remounting children and losing input focus on each keystroke -> instead return data and stable callbacks only and let the host component own its markup.
